Marcus: Finding Steady Ground

Marcus sits with his shoulders slightly forward, fingers drumming against his thigh in a rhythm he doesn't seem aware of. At thirty-three, he presents as younger than his years—there's a weariness in his face that speaks to something deeper than simple fatigue. He's a social media manager for a mid-sized nonprofit, work he describes as "manageable, predictable," though his wife has noticed he spends more time refreshing feeds at 3 a.m. than sleeping.

Three years ago, Marcus was different. He'd taken a leave from his job to work as a relief coordinator in a conflict zone in West Africa, driven by a sense of purpose he'd felt missing from his life. For eight months, he helped coordinate medical supplies, food distribution, and shelter for displaced families. It was meaningful work—grueling but meaningful. Then came the day that fractured everything.

A convoy he'd helped organize was struck by an IED. Marcus wasn't in the vehicle that took the direct hit, but he was close enough. He remembers the sound first—not the explosion itself, but the absence of sound afterward, a ringing void. He remembers running toward the smoke despite someone shouting his name. He remembers the faces of the people he'd worked with for months, people whose names he knew, whose families he'd heard about. Two of them didn't survive the ride to the hospital.

He returned home three weeks later, telling people he'd completed his service early due to a family matter. His wife, Amara, knew better. She watched him come back hollowed out, though he tried to hide it behind activity and normalcy.

The first months were the hardest. Marcus would wake gasping, convinced the walls were closing in. Amara learned to anticipate the bad nights—when he'd thrash in bed or suddenly leave to sit in the garage until dawn. He started having panic attacks at work, once in the middle of a team meeting about Instagram engagement metrics. The irony wasn't lost on him: he spent his days crafting narratives about the nonprofit's impact work, telling stories of hope and change, while internally he was fragmenting.

What troubles him most now is the unpredictability. He'll be scrolling through work emails when an image—a news report, a video, sometimes just a color palette—will transport him back. His heart races. His breathing becomes shallow. He finds himself checking the doors and windows, counting exits, assessing threats in spaces that are objectively safe. Amara has learned not to touch him suddenly during these episodes. She's learned to wait.

The guilt is perhaps the heaviest thing he carries. Why did he survive when others didn't? The question sits with him constantly. When his nonprofit celebrates successful campaigns, when colleagues praise his work managing their digital presence, he feels fraudulent. He's alive and curating content while people he knew are gone. The disconnect feels obscene.

He's started avoiding certain things—news from the region, conversations about international development, even some of his closest friends who ask how he's "really doing." He's become more withdrawn at home, though Amara insists she doesn't mind. He can see it in her eyes anyway: the concern, the exhaustion of loving someone who's partially unreachable.

Some days are better. He'll have stretches where the hypervigilance quiets, where he can sit through a meeting without his leg bouncing, where he doesn't wake up in a cold sweat. But he's learned not to trust the good days too much. They're always temporary. The weight is always there, just beneath the surface, waiting.
